layout_dets.text: Figure 1: We aim to build a foundation model for segmentation by introducing three interconnected components: a prompt-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Abstract

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We introduce the Segment Anything (SA) project: a new

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: task, model, and dataset for image segmentation. Using our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: efficient model in a data collection loop, we built the largest

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: segmentation dataset to date (by far), with over 1 billion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: masks on 11M licensed and privacy respecting images. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model is designed and trained to be promptable, so it can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transfer zero-shot to new image distributions and tasks. We

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evaluate its capabilities on numerous tasks and ind that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: its zero-shot performance is impressive – often competitive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with or even superior to prior fully supervised results. We

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are releasing the Segment Anything Model (SAM) and cor-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: responding dataset (SA-1B) of 1B masks and 11M images

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at segment-anything.com to foster research into foundation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: models for computer vision. We recommend reading the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: full paper at: arxiv.org/abs/2304.02643.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1. Introduction

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Large language models pre-trained on web-scale datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are revolutionizing NLP with strong zero-shot and few-shot

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generalization [10]. These “foundation models"[8] can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generalize to tasks and data distributions beyond those seen

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: during training. This capability is often implemented with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prompt engineering in which hand-crafted text is used to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prompt the language model to generate a valid textual re-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sponse for the task at hand. When scaled and trained with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: abundant text corpora from the web, these models'zero and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: few-shot performance compares surprisingly well to (even

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: matching in some cases) fine-tuned models [10, 20]. Empir-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ical trends show this behavior improving with model scale,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dataset size, and total training compute [54, 10, 20, 49].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Foundation models have also been explored in computer

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vision, albeit to a lesser extent. Perhaps the most promi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nent illustration aligns paired text and images from the web.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For example, CLIP [80] and ALIGN [53] use contrastive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learning to train text and image encoders that align the two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: modalities. Once trained, engineered text prompts enable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: zero-shot generalization to novel visual concepts and data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distributions. Such encoders also compose effectively with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: other modules to enable downstream tasks, such as image

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generation (e.g., DALL·E [81]). While much progress has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been made on vision and language encoders, computer vi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sion includes a wide range of problems beyond this scope,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and for many of these, abundant training data does not exist

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In this work, our goal is to build a foundation model for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image segmentation. That is, we seek to develop a prompt-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: able model and pre-train it on a broad dataset using a task

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that enables powerful generalization. With this model, we

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: aim to solve a range of downstream segmentation problems

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on new data distributions using prompt engineering.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The success of this plan hinges on three components:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: task, model, and data. To develop them, we address the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: following questions about image segmentation:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1. What task will enable zero-shot generalization?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. What is the corresponding model architecture?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3. What data can power this task and model?

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: These questions are entangled and require a comprehen-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sive solution. We start by defining a promptable segmenta-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion task that is general enough to provide a powerful pre-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training objective and to enable a wide range of downstream

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: applications. This task requires a model that supports flex-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ible prompting and can output segmentation masks in real-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: time when prompted to allow for interactive use. To train

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: our model, we need a diverse, large-scale source of data.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Unfortunately, there is no web-scale data source for seg-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mentation; to address this, we build a “data engine", i.e.,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we iterate between using our efficient model to assist in data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: collection and using the newly collected data to improve the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model. We introduce each interconnected component next,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: followed by the dataset we created and the experiments that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Task (§2). In NLP and more recently computer vision,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: foundation models are a promising development that can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perform zero-shot and few-shot learning for new datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and tasks often by using “prompting" techniques. Inspired

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by this line of work, we propose the promptable segmen-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tation task, where the goal is to return a valid segmenta-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion mask given any segmentation prompt (see Fig. 1a). A

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prompt simply specifies what to segment in an image, e.g.,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a prompt can include spatial or text information identifying

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an object. The requirement of a valid output mask means

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that even when a prompt is ambiguous and could refer to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: multiple objects (for example, a point on a shirt may in-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dicate either the shirt or the person wearing it), the output

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: should be a reasonable mask for at least one of those ob-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: jects. We use the promptable segmentation task as both a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pre-training objective and to solve general downstream seg-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mentation tasks via prompt engineering.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Model (§3). The promptable segmentation task and the goal

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of real-world use impose constraints on the model architec-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ture. In particular, the model must support flexible prompts,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: needs to compute masks in amortized real-time to allow in-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: teractive use, and must be ambiguity-aware. Surprisingly,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we find that a simple design satisfies all three constraints:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a powerful image encoder computes an image embedding,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a prompt encoder embeds prompts, and then the two infor-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mation sources are combined in a lightweight mask decoder

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that predicts segmentation masks. We refer to this model as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the Segment Anything Model, or SAM (see Fig. 1b). By

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: separating SAM into an image encoder and a fast prompt

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: encoder / mask decoder, the same image embedding can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be reused (and its cost amortized) with different prompts.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Given an image embedding, the prompt encoder and mask

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: decoder predict a mask from a prompt in ~50ms in a web

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: browser. We focus on point, box, and mask prompts, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also present initial results with free-form text prompts. To

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: make SAM ambiguity-aware, we design it to predict mul-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tiple masks for a single prompt allowing SAM to naturally

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: handle ambiguity, such as the shirt vs. person example.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Data engine (§4). To achieve strong generalization to new

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: data distributions, we found it necessary to train SAM on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a large and diverse set of masks, beyond any segmenta-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion dataset that already exists. While a typical approach

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for foundation models is to obtain data online [80], masks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: are not naturally abundant and thus we need an alternative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: strategy. Our solution is to build a “data engine", i.e., we

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: co-develop our model with model-in-the-loop dataset an-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: notation (see Fig. 1c). Our data engine has three stages:

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: assisted-manual, semi-automatic, and fully automatic. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the first stage, SAM assists annotators in annotating masks,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: similar to a classic interactive segmentation setup. In the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: second stage, SAM can automatically generate masks for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a subset of objects by prompting it with likely object lo-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cations and annotators focus on annotating the remaining

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: objects, helping increase mask diversity. In the final stage,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we prompt SAM with a regular grid of foreground points,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: yielding on average ~100 high-quality masks per image.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Dataset (§5). Our final dataset, SA-1B, includes more than

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1B masks from 11M licensed and privacy-preserving im-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ages (see Fig. 2). SA-1B, collected fully automatically us-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing the final stage of our data engine, has 400× more masks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: than any existing segmentation dataset [64, 43, 115, 58],

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and as we verify extensively, the masks are of high quality

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and diversity. Beyond its use in training SAM to be robust

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and general, we hope SA-1B becomes a valuable resource

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for research aiming to build new foundation models.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Experiments (§6). We extensively evaluate SAM. First, us-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing a diverse new suite of 23 segmentation datasets, we find

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that SAM produces high-quality masks from a single fore-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ground point, often only slightly below that of the manu-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ally annotated ground truth. Second, we find consistently

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: strong quantitative and qualitative results on a variety of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: downstream tasks under a zero-shot transfer protocol using

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prompt engineering, including edge detection, object pro-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: posal generation, instance segmentation, and a preliminary

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: exploration of text-to-mask prediction. These results sug-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gest that SAM can be used out-of-the-box with prompt en-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: gineering to solve a variety of tasks involving object and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image distributions beyond SAM's training data. Neverthe-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: less, room for improvement remains, as we discuss in §7.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Responsible AI. We provide model/dataset cards and report

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: on potential fairness concerns and biases when using SA-1B

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and SAM in the supplement. Images in SA-1B span a geo-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: graphically and economically diverse set of regions and we

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: found that SAM performs similarly across different groups

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of people. Together, we hope this will make our work more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: equitable for real-world use cases.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Release. We are releasing the SA-1B dataset for research

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: purposes and making SAM available under a permissive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: open license (Apache 2.0) at https://segment-anything.com.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We also showcase SAM's capabilities with an online demo.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 2: Example images with overlaid masks from our newly introduced dataset, SA-1B. SA-1B contains 11M diverse,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: high-resolution, licensed, and privacy protecting images and 1.1B high-quality segmentation masks. These masks were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: annotated fully automatically by SAM, and as we verify by human ratings and numerous experiments, are of high quality and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diversity. We group images by number of masks per image for visualization (there are ~100 masks per image on average).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 2. Segment Anything Task

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We take inspiration from NLP, where the next token pre-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: diction task is used for foundation model pre-training and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to solve diverse downstream tasks via prompt engineer-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing [10]. To build a foundation model for segmentation,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we aim to define a task with analogous capabilities.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Task. We start by translating the idea of a prompt from NLP

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to segmentation, where a prompt can be a set of foreground

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: / background points, a rough box or mask, free-form text,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or, in general, any information indicating what to segment

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in an image. The promptable segmentation task, then, is to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: return a valid segmentation mask given any prompt. The re-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quirement of a “valid" mask simply means that even when

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a prompt is ambiguous and could refer to multiple objects

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (e.g., recall the shirt vs. person example, and see Fig. 3),

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the output should be a reasonable mask for at least one of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: those objects. This requirement is similar to expecting a lan-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: guage model to output a coherent response to an ambiguous

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prompt. We choose this task because it leads to a natural

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pre-training algorithm and a general method for zero-shot

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transfer to downstream segmentation tasks via prompting.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Pre-training. The promptable segmentation task suggests a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: natural pre-training algorithm that simulates a sequence of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prompts (e.g., points, boxes, masks) for each training sam-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ple and compares the model's mask predictions against the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ground truth. We adapt this method from interactive seg-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mentation [107, 68], although unlike interactive segmenta-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion whose aim is to eventually predict a valid mask after

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: enough user input, our aim is to always predict a valid mask

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for any prompt even when the prompt is ambiguous. This

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ensures that a pre-trained model is effective in use cases that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: involve ambiguity, including automatic annotation as re-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quired by our data engine §4. We note that performing well

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at this task is challenging and requires specialized modeling

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and training loss choices, which we discuss in §3.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Zero-shot transfer. Intuitively, our pre-training task en-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dows the model with the ability to respond appropriately to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: any prompt at inference time, and thus downstream tasks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can be solved by engineering appropriate prompts. For ex-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ample, if one has a bounding box detector for cats, cat in-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stance segmentation can be solved by providing the detec-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tor's box output as a prompt to our model. In general, a wide

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: array of practical segmentation tasks can be cast as prompt-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing. In addition to automatic dataset labeling, we explore

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: five diverse example tasks in our experiments in §6.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Related tasks. Segmentation is a broad field: there's in-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: teractive segmentation [55, 107], edge detection [3], su-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: per pixelization [83], object proposal generation [2], fore-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ground segmentation [92], semantic segmentation [88], in-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stance segmentation [64], panoptic segmentation [57], etc.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The goal of our promptable segmentation task is to produce

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 3: Each column shows 3 valid masks generated by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: SAM from a single ambiguous point prompt (green circle).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a broadly capable model that can adapt to many (though

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not all) existing and new segmentation tasks via prompt

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: engineering. This capability is a form of task generaliza-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion [25]. Note that this is different than previous work on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: multi-task segmentation systems. In a multi-task system, a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: single model performs a fxed set of tasks, e.g., joint seman-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tic, instance, and panoptic segmentation [112, 18, 52], but

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the training and test tasks are the same. An important dis-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tinction in our work is that a model trained for promptable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: segmentation can perform a new, different task at inference

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: time by acting as a component in a larger system, e.g., to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: perform instance segmentation, a promptable segmentation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model is combined with an existing object detector.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Discussion. Prompting and composition are powerful tools

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that enable a single model to be used in extensible ways, po-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tentially to accomplish tasks unknown at the time of model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: design. This approach is analogous to how other founda-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion models are used, e.g., how CLIP [80] is the text-image

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alignment component of the DALL·E [81] image generation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: system. We anticipate that composable system design, pow-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ered by techniques such as prompt engineering, will enable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a wider variety of applications than systems trained specif-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ically for a fixed set of tasks. It's also interesting to com-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pare promptable and interactive segmentation through the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lens of composition: while interactive segmentation mod-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: els are designed with human users in mind, a model trained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for promptable segmentation can also be composed into a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: larger algorithmic system as we will demonstrate.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 4: Segment Anything Model (SAM) overview. A heavyweight image encoder outputs an image embedding that can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: then be efficiently queried by a variety of input prompts to produce object masks at amortized real-time speed. For ambiguous

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prompts corresponding to more than one object, SAM can output multiple valid masks and associated confidence scores.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3. Segment Anything Model

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We next describe the Segment Anything Model (SAM)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for promptable segmentation. SAM has three components,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: illustrated in Fig. 4: an image encoder, a flexible prompt

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: encoder, and a fast mask decoder. We build on Transformer

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: vision models [13, 32, 19, 60] with specific tradeoffs for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (amortized) real-time performance. We describe these com-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ponents at a high-level here, with details in §B.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Image encoder. Motivated by scalability and powerful pre-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training methods, we use an MAE [46] pre-trained Vision

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Transformer (ViT) [32] minimally adapted to process high

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: resolution inputs [60]. The image encoder runs once per

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image and can be applied prior to prompting the model.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Prompt encoder. We consider two sets of prompts: sparse

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (points, boxes, text) and dense (masks). We represent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: points and boxes by positional encodings [93] summed with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: learned embeddings for each prompt type and free-form text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with an off-the-shelf text encoder from CLIP [80]. Dense

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prompts (i.e., masks) are embedded using convolutions and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: summed element-wise with the image embedding.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mask decoder. The mask decoder efficiently maps the im-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: age embedding, prompt embeddings, and an output token

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to a mask. This design, inspired by [13, 19], employs a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: modification of a Transformer decoder block [101] followed

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by a dynamic mask prediction head. Our modified decoder

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: block uses prompt self-attention and cross-attention in two

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: directions (prompt-to-image embedding and vice-versa) to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: update all embeddings. After running two blocks, we up-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sample the image embedding and an MLP maps the output

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: token to a dynamic linear classifier, which then computes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the mask foreground probability at each image location.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Resolving ambiguity. With one output, the model will av-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: erage multiple valid masks if given an ambiguous prompt.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: To address this, we modify the model to predict multiple

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: output masks for a single prompt (see Fig. 3). We found

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 3 mask outputs is sufficient to address most common cases

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (nested masks are often at most three deep: whole, part, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subpart). During training, we backprop only the minimum

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: loss [14, 44, 62] over masks. To rank masks, the model pre-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dicts a confidence score (i.e., estimated IoU) for each mask.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Efficiency. The overall model design is largely motivated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by efficiency. Given a precomputed image embedding, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prompt encoder and mask decoder run in a web browser, on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: CPU, in ~50ms. This runtime performance enables seam-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: less, real-time interactive prompting of our model.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Losses and training. We supervise mask prediction with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the linear combination of focal loss [63] and dice loss [71]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: used in [13]. We train for the promptable segmentation task

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: using a mixture of geometric prompts (for text prompts see

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: §6.2). Following [90, 36], we simulate an interactive setup

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: by randomly sampling prompts in 11 rounds per mask, al-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lowing SAM to integrate seamlessly into our data engine.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 4. Segment Anything Data Engine

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: As segmentation masks are not abundant on the inter-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: net, we built a data engine to enable the collection of our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1.1B mask dataset, SA-1B. The data engine has three

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stages: (1) a model-assisted manual annotation stage, (2) a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: semi-automatic stage with a mix of automatically predicted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: masks and model-assisted annotation, and (3) a fully auto-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: matic stage in which our model generates masks without

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: annotator input. We go into details of each next.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Assisted-manual stage. In the first stage, resembling clas-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sic interactive segmentation, a team of professional annota-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tors labeled masks by clicking foreground / background ob-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ject points using a browser-based interactive segmentation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tool powered by SAM. Masks could be refined using pixel-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precise “brush" and “eraser" tools. Our model-assisted an-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: notation runs in real-time directly inside a browser (using

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: precomputed image embeddings) enabling a truly interac-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tive experience. We did not impose semantic constraints for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: labeling objects, and annotators freely labeled both “stuff"

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and "things"[1]. We suggested annotators label objects

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: they could name or describe, but did not collect these names

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: or descriptions. Annotators were asked to label objects in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: order of prominence and were encouraged to proceed to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: next image once a mask took over 30 seconds to annotate.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: At the start of this stage, SAM was trained using com-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mon public segmentation datasets. After sufficient data an-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: notation, SAM was retrained using only newly annotated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: masks. As more masks were collected, the image encoder

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: was scaled from ViT-B to ViT-H and other architectural de-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tails evolved; in total we retrained our model 6 times. Av-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: erage annotation time per mask decreased from 34 to 14

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: seconds as the model improved. We note that 14 seconds

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is 6.5× faster than mask annotation for COCO [64] and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: only 2× slower than bounding-box labeling with extreme

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: points [74, 69]. As SAM improved, the average number of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: masks per image increased from 20 to 44 masks. Overall,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: we collected 4.3M masks from 120k images in this stage.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Semi-automatic stage. In this stage, we aimed to increase

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the diversity of masks in order to improve our model's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ability to segment anything. To focus annotators on less

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prominent objects, we first automatically detected confident

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: masks. Then we presented annotators with images prefilled

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with these masks and asked them to annotate any additional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: unannotated objects. To detect confident masks, we trained

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a bounding box detector [82] on all first stage masks using a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: generic “object" category. During this stage we collected an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: additional 5.9M masks in 180k images (for a total of 10.2M

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: masks). As in the first stage, we periodically retrained our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model on newly collected data (5 times). Average annota-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion time per mask went back up to 34 seconds (excluding

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the automatic masks) as these objects were more challeng-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing to label. The average number of masks per image went

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from 44 to 72 masks (including the automatic masks).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fully automatic stage. In the final stage, annotation was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fully automatic. This was feasible due to two major en-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: hancements to our model. First, at the start of this stage, we

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: had collected enough masks to greatly improve the model,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: including the diverse masks from the previous stage. Sec-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ond, by this stage we had developed the ambiguity-aware

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: model, which allowed us to predict valid masks even in am-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: biguous cases. Specifically, we prompted the model with a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 32×32 regular grid of points and for each point predicted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a set of masks that may correspond to valid objects. With

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the ambiguity-aware model, if a point lies on a part or sub-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: part, our model will return the subpart, part, and whole ob-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ject. The IoU prediction module of our model is used to se-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lect confident masks; moreover, we identified and selected

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: only stable masks (we consider a mask stable if threshold-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing the probability map at 0.5 – δ and 0.5 + δ results in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: similar masks). Finally, after selecting the confident and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stable masks, we applied non-maximal suppression (NMS)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to filter duplicates. To further improve the quality of smaller

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: masks, we also processed multiple overlapping zoomed-in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image crops. For further details of this stage, see §C. We

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: applied fully automatic mask generation to all 11M images

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in our dataset, producing a total of 1.1B high-quality masks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: We describe and analyze the resulting dataset, SA-1B, next

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 5: Image-size normalized mask center distributions.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 5. Segment Anything Dataset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Our dataset, SA-1B, consists of 11M diverse, high-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: resolution, licensed, and privacy protecting images and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 1.1B high-quality segmentation masks collected with our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: data engine. We compare SA-1B with existing datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and analyze mask quality and properties. We are releasing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: SA-1B to aid future development of foundation models for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: computer vision. We note that SA-1B will be released un-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: der a favorable license agreement for certain research uses

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and with protections for researchers.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Images. We licensed a new set of 11M images from a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: provider that works directly with photographers. These im-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ages are high resolution (3300×4950 pixels on average),

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and the resulting data size can present accessibility and stor-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: age challenges. Therefore, we are releasing downsampled

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: images with their shortest side set to 1500 pixels. Even af-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ter downsampling, our images are significantly higher reso-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lution than many existing vision datasets (e.g., COCO [64]

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: images are ~480×640 pixels). Note that most models today

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: operate on much lower resolution inputs. Faces and vehicle

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: license plates have been blurred in the released images.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Masks. Our data engine produced 1.1B masks, 99.1% of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which were generated fully automatically. Therefore, the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: quality of the automatic masks is centrally important. We

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: compare them directly to professional annotations and look

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at how various mask properties compare to prominent seg-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mentation datasets. Our main conclusion, as borne out in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the analysis below and the experiments in §6, is that our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: automatic masks are high quality and effective for training

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: models. Motivated by these findings, SA-1B only includes

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: automatically generated masks.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mask quality. To estimate mask quality, we randomly sam-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pled 500 images (~50k masks) and asked our professional

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: annotators to improve the quality of all masks in these im-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ages. Annotators did so using our model and pixel-precise

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: “brush" and “eraser" editing tools. This procedure resulted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in pairs of automatically predicted and professionally cor-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rected masks. We computed IoU between each pair and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: found that 94% of pairs have greater than 90% IoU (and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 97% of pairs have greater than 75% IoU). For comparison,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prior work estimates inter-annotator consistency at 85-91%

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: IoU [43, 58]. Our experiments in §6 confirm by human rat-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ings that mask quality is high relative to a variety of datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and that training our model on automatic masks is nearly as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: good as using all masks produced by the data engine.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 6: Dataset mask properties. The legend references the number of images and masks in each dataset. Note, that SA-1B

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: has 11 × more images and 400× more masks than the largest existing segmentation dataset Open Images [58].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Mask properties. In Fig. 5 we plot the spatial distribution

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of object centers in SA-1B compared to the largest existing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: segmentation datasets. Common photographer biases are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: present in all datasets. We observe that SA-1B has greater

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: coverage of image corners compared to LVIS v1 [43] and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ADE20K [115], the two most similarly distributed datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: while COCO [64] and Open Images V5 [58] have a more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prominent center bias. In Fig. 6 (legend) we compare these

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: datasets by size. SA-1B has 11× more images and 400×

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more masks than the second largest, Open Images. On av-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: erage, it has 36× more masks per image than Open Images.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The closest dataset in this respect, ADE20K, still has 3.5×

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fewer masks per image. Fig. 6 (left) plots the masks-per-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image distribution. Next, we look at image-relative mask

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: size (square root of the mask area divided by image area)

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in Fig. 6 (middle). As expected, since our dataset has more

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: masks per image, it also tends to include a greater percent-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: age of small and medium relative-size masks. Finally, to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: analyze shape complexity, we look at mask concavity (1

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: minus mask area divided by area of mask's convex hull) in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fig. 6 (right). Since shape complexity is correlated with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mask size, we control for the datasets’ mask size distribu-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tions by first performing stratified sampling from binned

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mask sizes. We observe that the concavity distribution of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: our masks is broadly similar to that of other datasets.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 6. Zero-Shot Transfer Experiments

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In this section, we present zero-shot transfer experiments

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with SAM, the Segment Anything Model. We consider five

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tasks, four of which differ significantly from the promptable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: segmentation task used to train SAM. These experiments

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evaluate SAM on datasets and tasks that were not seen dur-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing training (our usage of “zero-shot transfer"follows its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: usage in CLIP [80]). The datasets may include novel image

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distributions, such as underwater or ego-centric images that,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to our knowledge, do not appear in SA-1B.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Our experiments begin by testing the core goal of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: promptable segmentation: producing a valid mask from any

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prompt. We emphasize the challenging scenario of a single

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: foreground point prompt, since it is more likely to be am-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: biguous than other more specific prompts. Next, we present

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a sequence of experiments that traverse low, mid, and high-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: level image understanding and roughly parallel the histori-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cal development of the field. Specifically, we prompt SAM

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to (1) perform edge detection, (2) segment everything, i.e.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: object proposal generation, (3) segment detected objects,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: i.e. instance segmentation, and (4), as a proof-of-concept,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to segment objects from free-form text. These four tasks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: differ significantly from the promptable segmentation task

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that SAM was trained on and are implemented via prompt

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: engineering. We report zero-shot single point valid mask

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: evaluation and zero-shot text to mask proof-of-concept in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the main text. We refer readers to the supplement for our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: experiments with zero-shot edge detection, object proposal,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and instance segmentation. In addition, we report a set of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ablations in the supplement. We analyze SAM performance

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with respect to the size and composition of its training data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as well as the image encoder architecture.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Implementation. Unless otherwise specified: (1) SAM

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: uses an MAE [46] pre-trained ViT-H [32] image encoder

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and (2) SAM was trained on SA-1B, noting that this dataset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: includes only automatically generated masks from the final

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stage of our data engine. For all other model and training

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: details, such as hyperparameters, refer to §B.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 6.1. Zero-Shot Single Point Valid Mask Evaluation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Task. We evaluate segmenting an object from a single fore-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ground point. This task is ill-posed as one point can refer

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to multiple objects. Ground truth masks in most datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: do not enumerate all possible masks, which can make au-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tomatic metrics unreliable. Therefore, we supplement the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: standard mIoU metric (i.e., the mean of all IoUs between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: predicted and ground truth masks) with a human study in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which annotators rate mask quality from 1 (nonsense) to 10

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (pixel-perfect). See §E.1, §F, and §H for additional details.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: By default, we sample points from the “center" of ground

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: truth masks (at a maximal value of the mask's interior dis-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tance transform), following the standard evaluation proto-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: col in interactive segmentation [90]. Since SAM is capable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of predicting multiple masks, we evaluate only the model's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: most confident mask by default. The baselines are all

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: single-mask methods. We compare mainly to RITM [90],

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a strong interactive segmenter that performs best on our

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: benchmark compared to other strong baselines [65, 17].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Datasets. We use a newly compiled suite of 23 datasets

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with diverse image distributions, see appendix Table 4 for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more details. We use all 23 datasets for mIoU evaluation.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For the human study, we use the subset listed in Fig. 7c

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (due to the resource requirements of such studies). This

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: subset includes both datasets for which SAM outperforms

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: and underperforms RITM according to automatic metrics.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Results. First, we look at automatic evaluation on the full

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: suite of 23 datasets using mIoU. We compare per-dataset

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: results in Fig. 7b against RITM. SAM yields higher re-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sults on 16 of the 23 datasets, by as much as ~47 IoU. We

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also present an “oracle" result, in which the most relevant

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of SAM's 3 masks is selected by comparing them to the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ground truth, rather than selecting the most confident mask.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This reveals the impact of ambiguity on automatic evalu-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ation. In particular, with the oracle to perform ambiguity

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: resolution, SAM outperforms RITM on all datasets.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Results of the human study are presented in Fig. 7c. Er-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ror bars are 95% confidence intervals (all differences are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: significant; see §F for details). We observe that the annota-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tors consistently rate the quality of SAM's masks substan-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tially higher than the strongest baseline, RITM. An ablated,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: “ambiguity-unaware" version of SAM with a single output

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mask has consistently lower ratings. SAM's mean ratings

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fall between 7 and 9, which corresponds to the qualitative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: rating guideline: “A high score (7-9): The object is identi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: fable and errors are small and rare (e.g., missing a small,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: heavily obscured disconnected component, ...)." These re-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: sults indicate that SAM has learned to segment valid masks

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: from a single point. Note that for datasets like DRAM and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: IBD, where SAM is worse on automatic metrics, it receives

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consistently higher ratings in the human study.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fig. 7d shows additional baselines, SimpleClick [65] and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: FocalClick [17]. As the number of points increases from 1

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to 9, we observe that the gap between methods decreases.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: This is expected as the task becomes easier; also, SAM is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not optimized for the very high IoU regime. Finally, in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Fig. 7e we replace the default center point sampling with

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: random point sampling. We observe that the gap between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: SAM and the baselines grows and SAM is able to achieve

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: comparable results under either sampling method.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 8: Zero-shot text-to-mask. SAM can work with sim-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ple and nuanced text prompts. When SAM fails to make a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: correct prediction, an additional point prompt can help.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 6.2. Zero-Shot Text-to-Mask

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Approach. This experiment is a proof-of-concept of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: SAM's ability to segment objects from free-form text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prompts. While we used the exact same SAM in all prior

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: experiments, for this one SAM's training procedure is mod-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ified to make it text-aware, but in a way that does not require

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: new text annotations. Specifically, for each manually col-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lected mask with area larger than 100² we extract the CLIP

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image embedding. Then, during training, we prompt SAM

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with the extracted CLIP image embeddings as its first in-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: teraction. The key observation here is that because CLIP's

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: image embeddings are trained to align with its text embed-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dings, we can train with image embeddings, but use text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: embeddings for inference. That is, at inference time we run

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: text through CLIP's text encoder and then give the resulting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: text embedding as a prompt to SAM (see §E.5 for details).

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Results. We show qualitative results in Fig. 8. SAM

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can segment objects based on simple text prompts like “a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: wheel" as well as phrases like “beaver tooth grille". When

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: SAM fails to pick the right object from a text prompt only,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: an additional point often fixes the prediction, similar to [30].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 7. Discussion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Foundation models. Pre-trained models have been adapted

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to downstream tasks since the early days of machine learn-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ing [97]. This paradigm has become increasingly impor-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tant in recent years with a growing emphasis on scale, and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such models have recently been (re-)branded as “founda-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion models": i.e. models that are “trained on broad data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at scale and are adaptable to a wide range of downstream

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tasks" [8]. Our work correlates well with this definition,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: though we note that a foundation model for image segmen-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tation is an inherently limited scope, since it represents an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: important, yet fractional, subset of computer vision. We

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: also contrast one aspect of our approach with [8], which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: emphasizes the role of self-supervised learning in founda-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion models. While our model is initialized with a self-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: supervised technique (MAE [46]), the vast majority of its

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: capabilities come from large-scale supervised training. In

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cases where data engines can scale available annotations,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: like ours, supervised training provides an effective solution.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Compositionality. Pre-trained models can power new ca-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pabilities even beyond ones imagined at the moment of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: training. One prominent example is how CLIP [80] is used

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: as a component in larger systems, such as DALL·E [81].

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Our goal is to make this kind of composition straightfor-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ward with SAM. We aim to achieve this by requiring SAM

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to predict a valid mask for a wide range of segmentation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: prompts. The effect is to create a reliable interface between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: SAM and other components. For example, MCC [104] can

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: easily use SAM to segment an object of interest and achieve

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: strong generalization to unseen objects for 3D reconstruc-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tion from a single RGB-D image. In another example, SAM

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: can be prompted with gaze points detected by a wearable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: device, enabling new applications. Thanks to SAM's abil-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ity to generalize to new domains like ego-centric images,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: such systems work without need for additional training.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Limitations. While SAM performs well in general, it is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not perfect. It can miss fine structures, hallucinates small

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: disconnected components at times, and does not produce

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: boundaries as crisply as more computationally intensive

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: methods that “zoom-in", e.g. [17]. In general, we expect

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: dedicated interactive segmentation methods to outperform

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: SAM when many points are provided, e.g. [65]. Unlike

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: these methods, SAM is designed for generality and breadth

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of use rather than high IoU interactive segmentation. More-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: over, SAM can process prompts in real-time, but neverthe-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: less SAM's overall performance is not real-time when using

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a heavy image encoder. Our foray into the text-to-mask task

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: is exploratory and not entirely robust, although we believe

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: it can be improved with more effort. While SAM can per-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: form many tasks, it is unclear how to design simple prompts

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that implement semantic and panoptic segmentation. Fi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nally, there are domain-specific tools, such as [7], that we

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: expect to outperform SAM in their respective domains.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Conclusion. The Segment Anything project is an attempt to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: lift image segmentation into the era of foundation models.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Our principal contributions are a new task (promptable seg-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mentation), model (SAM), and dataset (SA-1B) that make

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this leap possible. Whether SAM achieves the status of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: foundation model remains to be seen by how it is used in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the community, but regardless we expect the perspective of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: this work, the release of over 1B masks, and our promptable

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: segmentation model will help pave the path ahead.
